title: How to Connect Microsoft IQ to Existing Workflows
summary: Microsoft IQ is Microsoft's new automation platform for enterprise AI workflows. Identify which existing platforms it affects or whether to migrate.
body_markdown:
## What four questions define connecting a context source


### What connecting Microsoft IQ requires in any tool


Connecting any new context source to an existing workflow comes down to the same four questions. Who is the caller, what is that caller allowed to read, how does a request reach the endpoint, and what happens when the call fails or returns something unexpected?


The answers matter more than the tool.


A workflow that runs unattended at 3 a.m. can't prompt a person to sign in, so it needs an identity of its own, and the data it can reach is then bounded by what that identity was granted rather than by what the person who built the flow could see.


None of this is specific to Microsoft IQ, and none of it is something Microsoft's pages say about IQ. It is the checklist any team would run for a new endpoint, and it tells you which documentation gaps in the table above will bite first.


### Four ways to make the connection


The first is to stay inside the vendor's own automation tooling. For Microsoft services that usually means the automation products Microsoft already ships for its own ecosystem.


The appeal is that identity, licensing and audit sit in one place, and the cost is that the workflow lives wherever that tool lives, which matters if your approval chain or ticket queue runs elsewhere.


The second is a general-purpose automation platform that connects many vendors through ready-made steps. Zapier, Make, n8n and similar platforms all work this way.


You trade the vendor's single control plane for the ability to join Microsoft data to the rest of your stack, and you rely on the platform having a step for the service or on a generic HTTP step when it doesn't.


The third is to let an agent call the endpoint directly. Because MCP is an open protocol, an MCP-capable client can talk to an MCP server without any workflow engine in between.


That suits exploratory, conversational use, but it leaves scheduling, retries, approvals and logging to you, which is the work an automation platform exists to do.


The fourth is a small custom service that you write and host yourself. It gives full control over authentication, caching and error handling, and it is the most to build and maintain.


Teams usually choose it when the call sits inside a latency-sensitive path or when compliance rules out a third-party runner.


### How to choose a tool for Microsoft IQ


Start from where the workflow already runs. If the trigger, the approvals and the downstream systems already live in one tool, extend that tool before adding a second one, because every extra hop is another credential and another place a failure can hide.


Then match the approach to how much of the contract you can see. With a documented endpoint, a generic HTTP step or a custom service is straightforward.


Without one, which is the position today for Microsoft IQ, any approach is a prototype against an unconfirmed surface, and the cheapest one to throw away is the right one to start with.


Whichever you pick, keep the new call behind a single named connection, log what it returned, and make the step safe to run twice. Those three habits make a workflow easier to audit and cheaper to repair once the real documentation arrives.
